lesson.text: Quick memory: in grade 6 you learnt about smoking and vaping. Why is it so hard to stop? (Nicotine is addictive.) Today: what drugs are, their risks, what the law says, and where to get help.

A drug is any substance that changes how the body or mind works. Medicines are drugs that help when used as the label or a doctor says. Caffeine, nicotine and alcohol are legal for adults, and they still carry risks.

Illegal drugs are against the law to have, to give or to sell, and other countries have their own laws. Nobody checks what is in them or how strong they are. Mixing drugs, or drugs and alcohol, adds to the danger.

The risks: harm to the heart, the brain and mental health; accidents and bad decisions; trouble at school, with family and with the law. Breathing in gas, glue or aerosols can stop the heart, even the first time.

UK law: the Misuse of Drugs Act 1971 puts illegal drugs into classes A, B and C. Class A drugs are judged the most harmful and carry the heaviest punishments. Having one is possession; passing one on, even free, is supply.
Most young people never take illegal drugs. If someone offers you something, you can say no clearly, give a reason or another idea, and walk away. Real friends accept a no.

Getting help: talk to a trusted adult, your doctor or the school nurse. FRANK gives free, confidential advice on 0300 123 6600 (UK), and Childline is on 0800 1111. If someone is very unwell, call 999 at once.

Try it in the world: build a help board in your village with the numbers for FRANK, Childline and 999. In LIFE, Calm Corner practises saying no to pressure. For real: practise a clear 'No thanks' with a friend. Next: resolving conflicts.

exercises.prompt: A medicine is a kind of drug.
exercises.hint: A drug is anything that changes how the body or mind works.
exercises.explain: True: medicines are drugs that help when they are used as directed.

exercises.prompt: Who should give you a medicine?
choices: a trusted adult, as the label says
yourself, as much as you like
exercises.hint: Think about who can read the label and check it is right for you.
exercises.explain: A trusted adult, the way the label or the doctor says.

exercises.prompt: Match each word to its meaning.
matches: a drug that helps when ill
exercises.hint: Which words are about the law, and which about help?
exercises.explain: Possession: having one. Supply: passing one on. Medicine: helps when ill. Confidential: kept private.

exercises.hint: Which ones can adults buy in a shop?
exercises.explain: Legal for adults: caffeine, alcohol, nicotine (and they still carry risks). Illegal: class A and class B drugs.

exercises.prompt: Breathing in gas or aerosol sprays can stop the heart, even the first time.
exercises.hint: Think about how strongly some chemicals affect the heart.
exercises.explain: True: it can stop the heart suddenly, even the very first time.

exercises.prompt: Put a clear refusal in order.
items: give a reason, if you want
exercises.hint: Say it, back it up, change the plan, leave, then talk to someone.
exercises.explain: No thanks, a reason, another idea, walk away, and tell a trusted adult.

exercises.prompt: A friend gives you a pill 'for free'. In UK law, what has the friend done?
choices: supplied a drug, which is a crime
nothing wrong, as it was free
exercises.hint: Does it matter whether money changed hands?
exercises.explain: Passing on an illegal drug, even free, is supply: a crime.

exercises.prompt: You can tell how strong an illegal drug is by looking at it.
exercises.hint: Who checks what goes into an illegal drug?
exercises.explain: False: nobody checks, so its strength and contents are unknown.

exercises.prompt: Match each kind of help to its number.
exercises.hint: Which is about drugs, which for any worry, which for danger now?
exercises.explain: FRANK: 0300 123 6600. Childline: 0800 1111. Emergency: 999 or 112. Urgent but not an emergency: 111.

exercises.prompt: A risk to the body and mind, or to the future?
exercises.hint: Is it about health now, or what happens later?
exercises.explain: Body and mind: the heart, mental health, accidents. The future: a criminal record, trouble at school.

exercises.prompt: Why is mixing drugs, or drugs and alcohol, extra dangerous?
choices: their effects can add up unexpectedly
exercises.hint: Two things that each slow the body down: what happens together?
exercises.explain: Their effects can add up in ways nobody expects, which is why mixing is so risky.

exercises.prompt: Class A drugs carry the heaviest punishments because they are judged…
exercises.hint: What does the law sort the classes by?
exercises.explain: The classes go by harm: class A drugs are judged the most harmful, so having or supplying them brings the heaviest punishments.

exercises.prompt: Telling a trusted adult about a friend who takes drugs is getting them into trouble.
exercises.hint: What is the adult's job when someone is at risk?
exercises.explain: False: it is helping. A trusted adult can get your friend support, keep them safe, and help you too.

exercises.prompt: Someone has taken something and is breathing but won't wake up. After calling 999, what do you do?
choices: put them in the recovery position
put them in a cold shower
leave them to sleep it off
exercises.hint: Which keeps their airway open until help comes?
exercises.explain: The recovery position keeps the airway open so they can breathe. Stay with them, and tell the paramedics what they took.

exercises.prompt: Someone says, 'Everyone our age takes drugs.' What is true?
choices: most young people never take them
you must try to fit in
exercises.hint: Think about what most people really do.
exercises.explain: Most young people never take illegal drugs, so 'everyone does it' is false pressure: saying no is normal.

exercises.prompt: Match each part of the UK's law to what it means.
matches: can stop some jobs and travel
exercises.hint: The classes go by harm, A first.
exercises.explain: Class A: the most harmful, the heaviest penalties; B: heavy; C: lighter; a record can stop some jobs and travel.

exercises.prompt: In the UK, FRANK and Childline are free and confidential.
exercises.hint: Think about who these services are for.
exercises.explain: True: both are free and private, for anyone, any time.
